# Craft

- CRF-005: Classes follow SOLID: one reason to change (single responsibility), extended without being edited (open-closed), usable wherever their base type is (Liskov substitution), small interfaces shaped by their clients (interface segregation), and every dependency explicit, passed in as a constructor or method parameter, and pointing toward abstractions, never from business code to infrastructure details (dependency inversion, explicit dependencies).
- CRF-006: Keep concerns apart: business rules know nothing of UI, persistence or transport, and input is validated where it enters the system (a request, a message, a file, configuration), so the code inside can trust it; SEC-010 (proposed) says how an API validates a request.
- CRF-013: Wherever the tests run the app, the container validates scopes and its registrations (ValidateScopes, ValidateOnBuild) in every environment they use, not only in Development, so a singleton that captures a scoped service, and a scoped service resolved from the root, fail a test; the app's own setting is left as it is. CRF-020 holds Microsoft's dependency injection guidelines.
- CRF-014: Types limit outside access to their state: outside code changes an object's state through a well-defined function or property setter, not direct access to its private state (encapsulation). Types that need to be persisted stay unaffected by the persistence technology (persistence ignorance): a required base class, a required interface implementation, classes that save themselves, a required parameterless constructor, properties that must be virtual and persistence-specific required attributes all violate it. CRF-021 adds the kit's check on what the domain references.
- CRF-016: Objects have one responsibility and one reason to change (single responsibility). The direction of dependency is toward abstraction, not implementation details (dependency inversion). Methods and classes explicitly require the collaborating objects they need (explicit dependencies).
- CRF-017: Keep software separated by the kind of work it performs (separation of concerns): ideally business rules and logic reside in a separate project that doesn't depend on other projects in the application, and it helps if infrastructure concerns depend on abstractions defined in the business layer.
- CRF-018: Validate input before business processing or storage, and validate data from internal APIs, partner feeds, queues and stored records when it crosses a trust boundary.
- CRF-020: Follow Microsoft's dependency injection guidelines: avoid stateful, static classes and members; avoid instantiating dependent classes directly within services; avoid static access to services; avoid the service locator pattern and a factory that resolves dependencies at run time; avoid calling BuildServiceProvider while configuring services; enable scope validation so no singleton captures a scoped service; use the singleton lifetime only for services with their own state that is expensive to create or globally shared; and avoid the page's anti-patterns, a captive dependency and a scoped service retrieved outside a scope.
